guide.title: Use cases & guides
guide.intro: Practical recipes for common mocking tasks. Each one is a ready-to-run example — copy the curl, get a public URL, point your code at it.
guide.meta_description: Quickmock use cases: mock a REST API, test retry logic, simulate flaky or slow APIs, inspect webhooks, return fake data. Ready-to-run curl examples, free, no signup.
guide.inspector_note: Open the mock page and paste its admin token to watch incoming method, headers, query, and body in the private live inspector.
guide.cta.title: Build your own
home.usecases.title: Common use cases
home.usecases.body: Not sure where to start? See ready-to-run recipes for retry testing, flaky APIs, webhooks, and more.
guide.case.mock-rest-api.title: Mock a REST API endpoint
guide.case.mock-rest-api.summary: Get a public JSON endpoint to unblock your frontend before the backend exists.
guide.case.mock-rest-api.why: When the backend isn't ready, the frontend stalls. Stand up a mock that returns the exact JSON your UI expects, get a public URL, and build against it now — swap in the real API later.
guide.case.test-retry-logic.title: Test retry and back-off logic
guide.case.test-retry-logic.summary: A mock that fails first, then succeeds — so you can prove your retry code works.
guide.case.test-retry-logic.why: Retry code is notoriously untested because real APIs rarely fail on demand. This mock returns 500 on the first call and 200 on the second, then cycles, so an automated test can assert your client retries and recovers. The X-Mockapi-Variant header shows which step served each hit.
guide.case.simulate-flaky-api.title: Simulate a flaky API
guide.case.simulate-flaky-api.summary: Inject random errors and variable latency to catch bugs that only appear under load.
guide.case.simulate-flaky-api.why: Some bugs only surface when an upstream is unreliable. This mock fails a configurable share of requests with an alternate response and adds random latency in a min–max range, so your error handling and timeouts meet real-world chaos before production does.
guide.case.simulate-slow-api.title: Simulate a slow API
guide.case.simulate-slow-api.summary: Add a fixed delay to test loading states, spinners, and timeout handling.
guide.case.simulate-slow-api.why: A snappy localhost hides slow-network bugs. Give a mock a 3-second delay and watch how your UI behaves while it waits — and whether your client gives up at the right time.
guide.case.mock-webhook-receiver.title: Test a webhook receiver
guide.case.mock-webhook-receiver.summary: Catch incoming webhook calls and inspect their headers and body in real time.
guide.case.mock-webhook-receiver.why: Integrating a third-party webhook (Stripe, GitHub, a payment provider) means you need a URL to point it at — and a way to see exactly what it sends. Create a POST mock, give its URL to the provider, and watch every call land in the live request inspector: method, headers, query, body.
guide.case.mock-error-response.title: Mock a specific error response
guide.case.mock-error-response.summary: Return an exact 4xx/5xx status and body to reproduce an edge case on demand.
guide.case.mock-error-response.why: Reproducing a specific failure — a 422 with a particular validation payload, a 500, a 429 — is hard against a real API. Pin a mock to the exact status and body you need and point your code at it to verify it handles that case correctly.
guide.case.fake-json-data.title: Return realistic fake data
guide.case.fake-json-data.summary: Use {{faker.*}} tokens to get fresh names, emails, and UUIDs on every call.
guide.case.fake-json-data.why: Hard-coded sample data makes demos look fake and hides off-by-one bugs. Drop {{faker.name}}, {{faker.email}}, {{faker.uuid}} into the response body and the mock returns different realistic values on every hit — great for demos, seeding, and list/pagination UIs.
guide.case.echo-request-data.title: Echo the request back
guide.case.echo-request-data.summary: Reflect the incoming method, headers, and body into the response with {{request.*}} tokens.
guide.case.echo-request-data.why: Sometimes you need an endpoint that mirrors whatever it receives — to debug what your client actually sends, or to fake an API whose response depends on the request. The {{request.body}}, {{request.method}}, and {{request.header.*}} tokens echo the incoming request straight into the response.
guide.case.mock-api-with-cors.title: Mock an API with CORS
guide.case.mock-api-with-cors.summary: Create a public mock that browser JavaScript can call from any origin — no CORS errors, no proxy.
guide.case.mock-api-with-cors.why: When your frontend runs on localhost and the API is a mock on another origin, the browser blocks the fetch with a CORS error. Turn on CORS and Quickmock answers the preflight and adds permissive Access-Control-* headers, so fetch() just works from any origin while you build the UI. No credentials are exposed — the preset is wildcard-origin without Allow-Credentials.
Create a mock at work, then edit, delete, or clear its logs from home or CI using the one-time admin token from the create response.

Every created mock comes back with a one-time admin_token — save it, because it is never shown again. Editing, deleting, clearing logs, and reading the private inspector require that token: curl -X PUT https://quickmock.dev/api/mocks/<slug> -H 'Authorization: Bearer qm_...' -d '{...}'. The browser exchanges the same token for a path-scoped HttpOnly inspector session. Skip it and protected API calls return 401 admin_token_required; send the wrong value and they return 403 admin_token_invalid. The mock response URL remains public. Legacy mocks created before admin tokens keep their previous behavior until they expire.

docs.title: Quickmock API documentation
docs.meta_title: Quickmock API docs — variants, rules, routes and OpenAPI
docs.meta_description: Quickmock API reference with runnable curl examples for mock creation, named response variants, conditional rules, multi-route workspaces, OpenAPI import and private request logs.
docs.intro: Create one endpoint or a complete multi-route mock workspace through the JSON API. Every example below is copy-pasteable and uses the same contract as the web builder.
docs.create_body: POST /api/mocks returns the public URL and a one-time admin_token. Keep that token: updates, deletes and private logs require it as a Bearer token.
docs.variants_body: Variants make edge cases deterministic. Select one with X-Quickmock-Variant or __quickmock_variant; an unknown name falls back to normal matching.
docs.rules_body: Rules run in order and the first complete match wins. Sources: method, path, query, header and JSON body paths. Operators: equals, not_equals, contains and exists.
docs.routes_body: A single slug can expose up to 50 method + path routes. OpenAPI-style path placeholders such as {id} match one segment.
docs.privacy_body: Request logs are private by default. Choose whether bodies and sender IPs are retained; common credential headers are always redacted.
changelog.title: Changelog
changelog.intro: Technical changes shipped to Quickmock — features, fixes, security hardening. Source-of-truth is the git history; this page is the curated developer-facing view.
changelog.r0905.title: 2026-09-05 — Trusted client IP and relative-only redirects
changelog.r0905.security1: The client IP behind the per-IP mock limit, the IP blocklist, and the spam-filter allowlist is no longer read from a self-reported X-Forwarded-For header. It now comes from the immediate reverse proxy's own header (CF-Connecting-IP in production), and only when that peer is trusted — comma-separated forgeries are ignored outright.
changelog.r0905.security2: Breaking change: a mock's Location response header must now be a plain relative path (e.g. /m/abc123) — checked on the main response, named variants, routes, sequence steps, and the error response alike. Absolute URLs, protocol-relative //host, and backslash variants are rejected with 422 validation_failed on create and update; an existing row that still carries one has the header dropped on serve instead.
changelog.r0905.security3: Mock responses served from /m/:slug now send Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin, so a mock can no longer be loaded as a script, image, or iframe from another origin. A mock cannot override this header itself.
changelog.r0905.security4: The built-in anti-spam filter gained patterns for flag-file reads, secret-bearing environment lookups, loader and reverse-shell one-liners, cloud metadata paths, and two browser-hijacking idioms.
changelog.r0905.changed1: The admin token is now required on every mutating call — edit, delete, extend, and log export or clear — with no exception left for mocks created before tokens existed.
changelog.r0822.title: 2026-08-22 — Go 1.27 and CI refresh
changelog.r0822.changed1: The backend and production image now build with Go 1.27.0; the full race-tested suite continues to pass on the new toolchain.
changelog.r0822.changed2: GitHub Actions now uses Node.js 24-compatible checkout and setup-go releases, with the Go version sourced directly from go.mod to keep CI and production aligned.
changelog.r0819.title: 2026-08-19 — Deterministic scenarios, API workspaces and private logs
changelog.r0819.added1: Named response variants can now be selected explicitly with X-Quickmock-Variant or __quickmock_variant, making exact edge cases reproducible on demand.
changelog.r0819.added2: Ordered conditional rules select variants from the request method, path, query, headers, or JSON body using equals, not_equals, contains, and exists operators.
changelog.r0819.added3: One mock can now expose up to 50 method-and-path routes. Paste an OpenAPI 3.x JSON or YAML document into the builder to generate the workspace routes and example responses.
changelog.r0819.added4: New API documentation and a machine-readable OpenAPI 3.1 contract cover creation, variants, rules, workspaces, and inspector privacy.
changelog.r0819.security1: Request logs are private by default for new mocks. The admin token unlocks a path-scoped HttpOnly inspector session; creators can also disable storage of request bodies or sender IPs.
changelog.r0819.changed1: SEO/GEO metadata now publishes reciprocal language sitemap entries, includes the documentation page and updated freshness signals, and marks mock, workspace, sharing, and inspector URLs as non-indexable.
changelog.r0815.title: 2026-08-15 — Abuse resistance and safer mock responses
changelog.r0815.security1: The request inspector's fallback polling endpoints now have their own per-IP budget, limiting automated bursts without affecting normal live updates.
changelog.r0815.security2: Mock responses can no longer widen a service worker's scope, and redirect responses accept only relative, HTTP, or HTTPS destinations.
changelog.r0815.security3: The built-in abuse filter now rejects common SSRF primitives, executable handler configurations, and known backlink-page fingerprints. Self-hosters can also configure an IP/CIDR denylist.
changelog.r0815.fixed1: Container logs now rotate by default, and graceful shutdown no longer attempts to persist empty request-log records while draining a closed queue.
changelog.r0810.title: 2026-08-10 — Hardened mock creation from the browser
changelog.r0810.security1: Creating a mock from the site — the form on the home page and the one-click button on a template page — is now rejected when another site triggered it in your browser. Scripted access is unaffected: curl, CI jobs, and the public API send no browser origin headers and keep working exactly as before.
changelog.r0810.security2: Those same two actions now have their own rate-limit budget, separate from the one that serves mock traffic, so a runaway script can't spend your quota of active mocks.
changelog.r0810.changed1: The header no longer overflows on a phone: the Templates section made six links too many for one line, so the GitHub link moved down to the footer next to the other author links, and the remaining navigation wraps onto its own row instead of running off the screen.
changelog.r0810.changed2: Running your own instance: the server now warns at startup about environment variables left over from the old MOCKAPI_ prefix. Nothing has read them since the rename, so until now a stale key silently left the default in place — including QUICKMOCK_BASE_URL, which the new origin check depends on.
changelog.r0809.title: 2026-08-09 — Mock template gallery
changelog.r0809.added1: New /templates section: ten ready-made mock configurations across four categories (payments, developer tools, auth & identity, general purpose) — Stripe and Shopify webhooks, GitHub push events, Slack's url_verification handshake, OAuth2/OIDC discovery and JWKS, RFC 9457 error bodies, and more.
changelog.r0809.added2: Every template's "Create this mock" button creates it in one click, and the "Open it in the mock builder to tweak first" link opens the same config pre-filled in the regular mock form so you can adjust fields, headers, or status codes before saving.
changelog.r0809.added3: Each template page breaks down the payload's key fields and lists exactly how the mock differs from the real service it imitates — no pretending a static mock is the genuine API.
changelog.r0809.fixed1: The home page's "you've hit the active-mock limit" banner used to show the request-body size limit instead of the actual mock-count limit, plus a stray %!(EXTRA int=…) tail. It now shows the correct number with nothing extra appended.
changelog.r0726.title: 2026-07-26 — TTL cap, mock extension, log export
changelog.r0726.added1: A mock's lifetime is now capped: ttl_seconds can't exceed 30 days (server-configurable), whether set at creation or later.
changelog.r0726.added2: The mock page grows an "Extend" button that pushes the expiry further out, up to that same 30-day cap from the mock's creation date — it requires the admin token, same as editing or deleting the mock.
changelog.r0726.added3: Response body templates gained four tokens: {{random.pick:a|b|c}} picks one option per hit, {{seq}} counts hits, plus {{faker.price}} and {{faker.lorem}}.
changelog.r0726.added4: The request inspector can filter by HTTP method, and its "Download JSON" link now exports the full captured request/response history (including sender IPs) — requires the admin token, unlike the config export.
changelog.r0717.title: 2026-07-17 — Admin token per mock
changelog.r0717.added1: Creating a mock now returns a one-time admin token, shown once in a copyable banner on the mock page — save it, because it can't be shown again.
changelog.r0717.added2: Editing a mock, deleting it, or clearing its logs now needs that token: send it as Authorization: Bearer <token>. Reading a mock, its logs, and the live inspector still work by slug alone, no token required.
changelog.r0717.added3: Mocks created before this release keep working without a token until they expire. New guide: Manage mocks from any device.
changelog.r0705.title: 2026-07-05 — Live inspector, export & import, anti-spam
changelog.r0705.added1: The request inspector streams over Server-Sent Events: new requests appear instantly, with no polling, and the page falls back to polling automatically where SSE is unavailable.
changelog.r0705.added2: Export a mock's config as JSON from its page (no logs, no IPs) and import it on the create form — from a file or pasted text, entirely in your browser. The format matches POST /api/mocks, so exports are replayable via the API.
changelog.r0705.added3: An anti-spam content filter blocks abusive mock creation. Operators can replace the built-in pattern list (QUICKMOCK_SPAM_PATTERNS_FILE), disable it, or allowlist IPs (QUICKMOCK_SPAM_ALLOW_IPS).
changelog.r0619.title: 2026-06-19 — CORS toggle
changelog.r0619.added1: One checkbox on the create form turns on a permissive, credential-free CORS preset (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * and friends) and answers OPTIONS preflight with 204 — call a mock from browser JS on any origin, no proxy.
changelog.r0619.added2: New use-case guide: Mock an API with CORS.
changelog.r0613.title: 2026-06-13 — Use-case guides
changelog.r0613.added1: New /guide section: scenario-first landing pages for common tasks — mock a REST API, test retry logic, simulate flaky or slow APIs, inspect webhooks, return fake data, echo the request. Each page has a ready-to-run curl example; all are listed in the sitemap.
changelog.r0613.added2: Each guide now has a copy button on its curl examples and a one-click Create a mock CTA that opens the home form pre-filled with that recipe's config — method, body, delay, error rate, sequence — ready to submit.
changelog.r0611.title: 2026-06-11 — Flaky-API simulation
changelog.r0611.added1: Response sequences: a mock can now hold an ordered list of up to 10 extra responses (status + body + headers each) cycled per hit — 1st call → main response, 2nd → step 2, … then loop. Classic retry-logic testing. The position is a shared per-mock counter (Redis, with an in-process fallback), so every caller advances the same sequence.
changelog.r0611.added2: Error rate & delay jitter: a configurable share of requests (0–100%, rolled per request) can answer with an alternate status/body, and the response delay can be a min–max range for random latency jitter instead of a fixed value. All three settings combine, and a new X-Mockapi-Variant response header (default, error, or seq-i/n) shows which branch served each hit. Configurable from the create form (new “Flaky simulation” section) and the API.
changelog.r0611.added3: The “Who built this” section on the home page now links to the maintainer's personal site (deadsquirrel.dev), language-matched per locale.
changelog.r0610.title: 2026-06-10 — Request echo tokens
changelog.r0610.added1: New request.* dynamic tokens echo the incoming request back into the response body: {{request.method}}, {{request.path}}, {{request.ip}}, {{request.query.id}}, {{request.header.x-request-id}}, {{request.body}}, and JSON dot paths like {{request.body.user.name}}. Values are inserted verbatim and nothing extra is stored — a static mock can now answer with data from the request itself.
changelog.r0610.fixed1: The 2026-05-20 entry below used to display Go-template escaping ({{`…`}}) around every token instead of the token itself — leftover from copying the markup out of an HTML template. Now it shows plain {{faker.uuid}} and friends.
changelog.r0608.title: 2026-06-08 — Author link
changelog.r0608.added1: Footer credit now links the author name to the maintainer's personal site (deadsquirrel.dev), language-matched per locale, with rel="me" as an identity signal.
changelog.r0525.title: 2026-05-25 — Site content pass
changelog.r0525.added1: This /changelog page itself, in EN and RU, with hreflang and an entry in sitemap.xml.
changelog.r0525.added2: Home page: a Quick glossary section (Mock API, Endpoint, TTL, Faker token, Content-Type) for readers landing here without context.
changelog.r0525.added3: Home page: a Who built this block with author bio and direct links to GitHub, LinkedIn, Telegram — and a Why I built Quickmock personal-story section, so the page isn't a faceless tool landing.
changelog.r0525.added4: Visible Last updated stamp at the bottom of the home page; dateModified mirrored into the WebApplication JSON-LD so AI crawlers see freshness.
changelog.r0525.fixed1: ?lang=<code> in the URL now actually serves that language. Previously the canonical / hreflang links pointed at ?lang=ru but the resolver only read the cookie and Accept-Language, so a bot following the hreflang link saw English content — the multilingual signal was a lie.
changelog.r0523.security1: Origin hardening for /m/*: the public mock router now strips request-altering headers a malicious caller could use to confuse downstream proxies, slugs were lengthened (more entropy), and internal error messages are redacted before they reach the wire — no DSN fragments, no stack frames.
changelog.r0523.security2: Language switcher (POST /language) now accepts same-origin absolute Referers, so the redirect-back path works behind reverse proxies that rewrite the Referer header. Cross-origin Referers are still rejected.
changelog.r0523.fixed1: RealIP middleware now trusts X-Forwarded-For / X-Real-IP when the immediate peer is loopback or a private/link-local address. Previously XFF was honored only for loopback peers, so behind Docker Compose every request was attributed to the bridge gateway (e.g. 172.18.0.1) — making creator_ip and request_ip useless and turning the per-IP mock limit into a global one.
changelog.r0523.fixed2: Mock router now stores incoming request headers with lowercased keys, so request_headers->>'user-agent' works regardless of wire casing.
changelog.r0523.fixed3: UI: slug examples updated to the new 12-char format; Copy-URL button restored on the mock detail page.
changelog.r0521.title: 2026-05-21 — UGC disclaimer
changelog.r0521.added1: Footer disclaimer and Terms-of-use modal: mocks are user-generated content, prohibited categories (malware, phishing, CSAM, attack infrastructure) are spelled out, and an abuse-report channel is published.
changelog.r0521.added2: Footer modal stays usable on small viewports — close button is no longer clipped on mobile.
changelog.r0520.title: 2026-05-20 — Dynamic tokens
changelog.r0520.added1: Faker / now token substitution in response bodies: {{faker.uuid}}, {{faker.email}}, {{faker.name}}, {{now.iso8601}}, plus 18 more (people, IDs, network, text, time). The mock stores the template as-is and renders fresh random values on every hit, so one mock can serve different data per call. Full list lives under Dynamic tokens on the create form.
changelog.r0518.title: 2026-05-18 — Hardening & quality of life
changelog.r0518.fixed1: Docker Compose deploy now waits for the --wait healthcheck instead of polling /healthz in a shell loop, so deploys no longer print the cosmetic curl: (52) Empty reply while the proxy and Go process finish racing.
changelog.r0518.fixed2: POSTGRES_PASSWORD example in .env.example now warns against base64-encoded values — pgx's DSN parser chokes on + / = in the password.
changelog.r0517.title: 2026-05-17 — Initial public release
changelog.r0517.added1: Core mock engine: create, view, edit, delete; all HTTP methods including ANY.
changelog.r0517.added2: Public /m/:slug router with configurable status, body, headers, response delay (0–30 s), and TTL.
changelog.r0517.added3: Live request inspector: HTMX 2-second poll, per-mock counter, clear-logs.
changelog.r0517.added4: cURL import — paste a curl … command to pre-fill the create form.
changelog.r0517.added5: Code snippets on the mock detail page for JavaScript, Python, Go, and PHP.
changelog.r0517.added6: Read-only share preview at /share/:slug with Open Graph tags.
changelog.r0517.added7: Per-IP rate limit (5000 hits / 8 hours) and per-IP active-mock cap (50).
changelog.r0517.added8: 512 KB max response body, enforced by handler and a DB CHECK constraint.
changelog.r0517.added9: Docker Compose stack (app + Postgres + Redis + one-shot migration container) and a bare-metal systemd path.
changelog.r0517.added10: EN + RU localization, language switcher (cookie + Accept-Language).
changelog.r0517.added11: Privacy by design: no third-party JS, no analytics, no fonts CDN; CI enforces this on every build.

home.howto.title: How does Quickmock work?
home.howto.intro: Quickmock is an online mock API and REST endpoint generator: paste a JSON (or any) response body, pick an HTTP method and status code, and get a public URL you can call from anywhere — no signup, no install.
home.privacy.badge: No trackers · No analytics · No accounts
home.privacy.body: No third-party analytics. No tracking pixels. No fingerprinting. No external JS or fonts. No ads. No accounts, no email, no data sold or shared.
home.privacy.title: What I don't do
home.privacy.what_we_log.item1: Your IP for rate limiting — kept for 8 hours in Redis, then dropped.
home.privacy.what_we_log.item2: The IP that created a mock — to enforce the 50-mocks-per-IP limit. Never shown in the UI.
home.privacy.what_we_log.item3: Requests to your mocks — that's the private inspector. Body and sender-IP capture can be disabled; retained requests disappear with the mock.
home.privacy.what_we_log.item4: Language preference and, after admin-token verification, a path-scoped HttpOnly inspector session.
home.privacy.what_we_log.title: What I do log (and why)
home.security.body: Mocks are public — anyone with the URL can read the response body. Never put real API keys, access tokens, passwords, or production data into a mock.
home.security.title: Don't paste real secrets
home.author.title: Who built this
home.author.body: Quickmock is built and maintained by Nikita Chernykh — backend engineer / tech lead — as a free side project. The whole thing is open source on GitHub; the code, the schema, the deploy script — everything you see is in the repo.
home.story.title: Why I built Quickmock
home.story.body: Every team I've worked on has spent hours of dev time on the same problem: the frontend needs an endpoint that the backend hasn't built yet, or QA needs to reproduce a flaky 500, or someone wants to demo an API contract without spinning up a whole service. I kept reaching for hosted mock-API tools that demand a signup, a paid tier for anything past three endpoints, and a privacy policy I'd rather not read. Quickmock is what I wanted instead: a public URL in 30 seconds, no account, no tracking, real request inspector, fully open source.
home.glossary.title: Quick glossary
home.glossary.mock.def: A fake HTTP endpoint that returns a response you control — used to develop against an API before the real one exists, or to reproduce specific responses in tests.
home.glossary.endpoint.def: A single addressable URL on a server that accepts requests of a given method (GET, POST, …) and returns a response. Quickmock gives you one per mock.
home.glossary.ttl.def: Time-to-live — how long a mock stays alive before Quickmock deletes it. Pick 1 hour, 24 hours, 7 days, or 30 days at creation.
home.glossary.faker.def: A placeholder like `{{faker.email}}` or `{{now.iso8601}}` that Quickmock substitutes with a fresh random value on every request, so the same mock can return different data each call.
home.glossary.ct.def: The HTTP header that tells the client how to parse the response body — `application/json`, `application/xml`, `text/plain`, `text/html`.
mock.create.beautify_error: Cannot beautify — body isn't valid JSON.
mock.create.delay_jitter_hint: Fixed delay, or set max for random jitter in the min–max range. 0–30000 ms.
mock.create.flaky.title: Flaky simulation
mock.create.flaky.hint: Make the mock behave like an unstable API: random errors and a response sequence that changes on every call. Tokens like {{faker.uuid}} work in every body.
mock.create.flaky.error_rate_hint: This share of requests gets the alternate response below. 0 turns it off.
mock.create.flaky.seq_hint: Responses are served in order — step 1 is the main response above — then loop. The position is shared by all callers.
mock.create.flaky.step_headers_placehold: Extra headers, one per line: X-Header: value

seo.description: Quickmock — free HTTP mock API in 30 seconds. Pick method, status, body — get a public URL. Live request inspector. No signup, no tracking, open source.
seo.faq.a1: Quickmock is a free online tool that creates a public HTTP mock endpoint in 30 seconds. You paste a response body, pick a method and status code, and get a URL you can call from any client — curl, Postman, your frontend, a CI test, anywhere.
seo.faq.a2: No. There is no account, no email, no credit card. Mocks are limited per IP and expire after the TTL you pick (up to 30 days). The service is free and open source.
seo.faq.a3: Frontend prototyping while the backend is not ready, webhook testing, integration and contract tests, reproducing edge cases like 500 errors or slow responses, API demos, and teaching examples.
seo.faq.a4: Yes. Every mock has a private live inspector for incoming method, path, headers, query, and body. Unlock it with the mock's admin token; body and sender-IP capture can be disabled.
seo.faq.q2: Do I need to sign up or pay?
seo.faq.q3: What can I use Quickmock for?
seo.faq.a5: Yes. Drop tokens like {{faker.uuid}}, {{faker.name}}, {{faker.email}}, or {{now.iso8601}} into the response body — the mock stores the template as-is and substitutes fresh values on every hit. request.* tokens echo the incoming request back: {{request.query.id}}, {{request.header.x-request-id}}, {{request.body.user.name}}. The full list (people, IDs, network, text, time, request echo) is in the form under "Dynamic tokens".
seo.faq.q4: Can I see who calls my mock?
seo.faq.title: Frequently asked questions

templates.title: Mock templates
templates.intro: Ready-to-use mock configurations that reproduce the shape of a well-known webhook, API, or auth endpoint. Pick one and create it with a single click, or open it in the builder first to tweak it — either way, you get a working URL in seconds.
templates.meta_description: Ready-to-use Quickmock templates: Stripe, Shopify, GitHub, Slack, and Telegram webhooks, OAuth2/OpenID/JWKS endpoints, a paginated API, an error response. Free, no signup.
templates.kind.payload: Returns a ready-made event — feed it straight into your own handler.
templates.kind.responder: Accepts an incoming call and replies the way the service expects.
templates.kind.api: Stands in for a third-party API endpoint.
templates.section.differences: How this differs from the real thing
templates.cta.title: Ready to use it?
templates.cta.open_in_form: Open it in the mock builder to tweak first
templates.case.stripe-webhook.title: Mock a Stripe webhook payload
templates.case.stripe-webhook.summary: A GET mock that returns a Stripe-shaped payment_intent.succeeded event, ready to feed into your webhook handler.
templates.case.stripe-webhook.difference: This is a static event trimmed down from a real Stripe payload — no Stripe-Signature header, no live objects behind the IDs. Use it to shape your handler's parsing logic, not to test signature verification.
templates.case.stripe-webhook.field.id: A synthetic event ID — Stripe's real IDs follow the same evt_... shape but are never reused.
templates.case.stripe-webhook.field.type: The event type your handler switches on; change it to trigger a different code path.
templates.case.stripe-webhook.field.crea: Unix timestamp of the event, generated fresh on every call via {{now.unix}}.
templates.case.stripe-webhook.field.data: The charge amount in minor units (cents) — 4999 means $49.99.
The payment_intent status; edit the response body to test other states like requires_action.
templates.case.shopify-order-webhook.sum: A GET mock shaped like a Shopify order webhook, with an order_number that counts up and a random total and customer email.
templates.case.shopify-order-webhook.dif: This is one trimmed-down order instead of the full field set a real Shopify order carries, and the request isn't signed. order_number counts up via {{seq}}; total_price and customer.email are random on every call.
templates.case.shopify-order-webhook.fie: Counts up on every call via {{seq}} — this is how Shopify's own order numbers behave too.
A random amount via {{faker.price}}; a real order's total is the sum of its line items plus tax and shipping.
The currency code, hardcoded here to USD.
The order's line items — one fixed item here, a real order can carry many.
templates.case.github-webhook-push.title: Mock a GitHub push webhook
templates.case.github-webhook-push.summa: A GET mock shaped like a GitHub push event, with one commit on refs/heads/main.
templates.case.github-webhook-push.diffe: This is a single static commit rather than the full field set a real push event carries — no X-Hub-Signature-256 header, no sender or head_commit, no compare URL.
templates.case.github-webhook-push.field: The branch that was pushed to, e.g. refs/heads/main.
The commit SHA after the push — later GitHub API calls reference it.
The repository name as owner/repo; edit it to match your test repo.
The commits included in this push — trimmed to one here.
templates.case.slack-events-api.title: Mock the Slack Events API challenge
templates.case.slack-events-api.summary: A POST mock that answers Slack's url_verification handshake by echoing the challenge value back.
templates.case.slack-events-api.differen: The request signature (the X-Slack-Signature header) isn't checked — this mock echoes the same challenge back to anyone who sends a matching body, not only to Slack itself.
templates.case.slack-events-api.field.ch: Echoed straight from your request body via {{request.body.challenge}} — exactly what Slack's url_verification handshake checks for.
templates.case.telegram-bot-webhook.summ: A POST mock that replies to a Telegram Update with a sendMessage call back to the same chat.
templates.case.telegram-bot-webhook.diff: Telegram's webhook secret token isn't checked — this mock replies to anyone who posts a matching Update, not only to Telegram's own servers.
templates.case.telegram-bot-webhook.fiel: The Bot API method name that the webhook response itself performs.
Taken from the incoming Update via {{request.body.message.chat.id}}.
The reply text; edit it to test a different bot response.
templates.case.oauth2-token-response.sum: A POST mock that returns an RFC 6749-shaped token response with a fresh access_token and refresh_token.
templates.case.oauth2-token-response.dif: access_token and refresh_token are just fresh UUIDs, not real signed JWTs, and the mock never checks client_id, client_secret, or an authorization code — it always returns the same successful response.
templates.case.oauth2-token-response.fie: A fresh UUID on every call via {{faker.uuid}} — not a real signed token.
A hardcoded lifetime in seconds; edit it to test expiry handling.
Space-separated scopes granted; edit it to test scope-gated logic.
templates.case.openid-configuration.titl: Mock an OpenID Connect discovery document
templates.case.openid-configuration.summ: A GET mock at /.well-known/openid-configuration with issuer, authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint, and jwks_uri.
templates.case.openid-configuration.diff: Every URL in this document is a placeholder built from YOUR-SLUG — replace it with the mock's real https://quickmock.dev/m/<slug> URL before pointing a real OIDC client at it. Editing the response body needs the admin token from the create banner; see /guide/manage-mocks-from-any-device for how that works.
templates.case.openid-configuration.fiel: The issuer URL clients compare against a token's iss claim; it must exactly match the base URL.
Where a client sends the user to log in.
Where a client exchanges a code for tokens.
Where a client fetches the public keys — pairs with the jwks-endpoint template.
templates.case.jwks-endpoint.title: Mock a JWKS endpoint for JWT verification
templates.case.jwks-endpoint.summary: A GET mock at /.well-known/jwks.json returning one RSA key in JWK Set format.
templates.case.jwks-endpoint.differences: The RSA key in this document is illustrative only — Quickmock doesn't hold a matching private key, so it can never verify a real signature. Use it to check that your client parses a JWKS document correctly, not to validate real tokens.
templates.case.jwks-endpoint.field.keys: The JWK Set array; add more entries to test key-rotation logic.
The key ID a JWT's header would reference to pick this key.
The signing algorithm this key claims to support.
The RSA modulus, base64url-encoded — illustrative only, not a working key.
templates.case.paginated-collection.titl: Mock a paginated JSON API response
templates.case.paginated-collection.summ: A GET mock that returns a page of three fake records alongside page, per_page, total, and next.
templates.case.paginated-collection.diff: The three records are random and regenerate on every call instead of coming from a stable dataset, and next is a fixed string rather than a working link — replace YOUR-SLUG with the mock's real slug to make it usable.
templates.case.paginated-collection.fiel: An array of fake records, three per call via {{faker.*}} tokens.
The current page number, hardcoded to 1.
The total record count across all pages, hardcoded to 42.
The URL for the next page — edit YOUR-SLUG to the mock's real slug.
templates.case.problem-json-error.title: Mock an RFC 9457 problem+json error
templates.case.problem-json-error.summar: A GET mock that returns a 422 application/problem+json validation error shaped per RFC 9457.
templates.case.problem-json-error.differ: This is one fixed validation error — status, detail, and the errors[] extension are all hardcoded, so edit the response body to reproduce the exact failure your client needs to handle instead of a generic 422.
A URI identifying the problem type — it's a documentation address, not necessarily a working link.
A short, human-readable summary of the problem.
Mirrors the HTTP response status, kept in the body for clients that log it separately.
A specific explanation for this occurrence; edit it to match the failure you're testing.
A non-standard extension array with field-level errors, the kind GitHub- or Stripe-style APIs often add.
